5-1.title: Adjectives vs. Adverbs
5-1.learn:
HOW TO TELL ADJECTIVES FROM ADVERBS

An ADJECTIVE describes a NOUN (a person, place, or thing): 'a quick fox,' 'the happy child.'
An ADVERB describes a VERB, an adjective, or another adverb, and often ends in -ly: 'runs quickly,' 'very tall,' 'quite slowly.'

Example 1 — Adjective: 'She is a beautiful singer.'
'Beautiful' describes the noun 'singer,' so it is an adjective.

Example 2 — Adverb: 'She sings beautifully.'
'Beautifully' describes the verb 'sings' (HOW she sings), so it is an adverb.
Wrong: 'She sings beautiful.' You need the adverb form 'beautifully' to describe the action.

Example 3 — Test it: Ask what the word describes. If it describes a noun, it's an adjective ('a careful driver'). If it describes a verb/action, it's an adverb ('drives carefully').
Clue: Many adverbs end in -ly, but not all (fast, hard, well can be adverbs too).

questions.question: Which word is an ADJECTIVE in 'The tall boy waved.'?
questions.explanation: 'Tall' describes the noun 'boy,' so it is an adjective.

questions.question: Which word is an ADVERB in 'The dog barked loudly.'?
questions.explanation: 'Loudly' describes the verb 'barked' (HOW it barked), so it is an adverb.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'She sings ___.'
questions.explanation: An adverb is needed to describe the verb 'sings,' so 'beautifully' is correct.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The ___ runner won the race.'
questions.explanation: The adjective 'quick' describes the noun 'runner.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'He finished the test ___.'
questions.explanation: The adverb 'quickly' describes the verb 'finished' (HOW he finished).

questions.question: Which sentence uses the modifier correctly?
questions.explanation: The adverb 'clearly' correctly describes the verb 'speaks.'

questions.question: In 'The very bright light hurt my eyes,' what does 'very' describe?
questions.explanation: 'Very' is an adverb that describes the adjective 'bright,' telling how bright.

questions.question: Which sentence is CORRECT?
questions.explanation: 'Well' is the adverb that correctly describes how the team 'played'; 'good' is an adjective.

questions.question: Which sentence uses both an adjective and an adverb correctly?
questions.explanation: The adjective 'careful' describes the noun 'driver,' and the adverb 'carefully' describes the verb 'drove.'

questions.question: Which word is the adverb in 'The extremely tired hikers walked slowly home.'?
questions.explanation: 'Slowly' describes the verb 'walked' (HOW they walked), so it is an adverb. ('Extremely' is also an adverb, but it describes the adjective 'tired.')

questions.question: Which word is an ADJECTIVE in 'A cold wind blew.'?
questions.explanation: 'Cold' describes the noun 'wind,' so it is an adjective.

questions.question: Which word is an ADVERB in 'The turtle moved slowly.'?
questions.explanation: 'Slowly' describes the verb 'moved' (HOW it moved), so it is an adverb.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The ___ flowers smelled sweet.'
questions.explanation: The adjective 'bright' describes the noun 'flowers.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The crowd cheered ___.'
questions.explanation: The adverb 'loudly' describes the verb 'cheered' (HOW they cheered).

questions.question: Which word is an ADJECTIVE in 'A wise owl watched us.'?
questions.explanation: 'Wise' describes the noun 'owl,' so it is an adjective.

questions.question: Which word is an ADVERB in 'She quietly closed the door.'?
questions.explanation: 'Quietly' describes the verb 'closed' (HOW she closed it), so it is an adverb.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The painter worked ___ on the mural.'
questions.explanation: The adverb 'carefully' describes the verb 'worked' (HOW he worked).

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'It was a ___ morning.'
questions.explanation: The adjective 'peaceful' describes the noun 'morning.'

questions.question: Which word is an ADVERB in 'The baby cried softly.'?
questions.explanation: 'Softly' describes the verb 'cried' (HOW the baby cried), so it is an adverb.

questions.question: Which word is an ADJECTIVE in 'The ancient castle stood tall.'?
questions.explanation: 'Ancient' describes the noun 'castle,' so it is an adjective. ('Tall' here describes the castle too, but 'ancient' is the clearest noun-modifier in front of it.)

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The students answered the question ___.'
questions.explanation: The adverb 'correctly' describes the verb 'answered' (HOW they answered).

questions.question: Which sentence uses the modifier correctly?

choices.A: He drives careful in the rain.
choices.B: He drives carefully in the rain.
choices.C: He drives carefulness in the rain.
choices.D: He is a carefully driver in the rain.

questions.explanation: The adverb 'carefully' correctly describes the verb 'drives.'

questions.question: In 'The dancer moved gracefully across the stage,' what does 'gracefully' describe?
questions.explanation: 'Gracefully' tells HOW the dancer 'moved,' so it describes the verb 'moved.'

questions.question: In 'That was an unusually quiet class,' what does 'unusually' describe?
questions.explanation: 'Unusually' is an adverb describing the adjective 'quiet,' telling HOW quiet.

questions.question: Which sentence uses an ADJECTIVE correctly?

choices.D: The soup tastes deliciously good only.

questions.explanation: After the linking verb 'tastes,' the adjective 'delicious' describes the noun 'soup,' not the action.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The thunder was ___ loud last night.'
questions.explanation: The adverb 'extremely' describes the adjective 'loud,' telling HOW loud.

questions.question: Which word is the ADVERB in 'The wildly excited fans screamed.'?
questions.explanation: 'Wildly' describes the adjective 'excited,' telling HOW excited, so it is an adverb.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'She felt ___ after the long hike.'
questions.explanation: After the linking verb 'felt,' the adjective 'happy' describes the subject 'She,' not the action.

questions.question: Which sentence uses 'good' and 'well' correctly?

choices.A: She is a good singer who sings good.
choices.B: She is a well singer who sings good.
choices.C: She is a good singer who sings well.
choices.D: She is a well singer who sings well.

questions.explanation: The adjective 'good' describes the noun 'singer,' and the adverb 'well' describes the verb 'sings.'

questions.question: Which sentence is CORRECT?

choices.D: The engine is a smoothly runner now.

questions.explanation: The adverb 'smoothly' describes the verb 'runs' (HOW the engine runs).

questions.question: Which word is an ADJECTIVE in 'The fast train arrived early.'?
questions.explanation: 'Fast' describes the noun 'train,' so here it is an adjective. ('Early' describes the verb 'arrived,' so it is an adverb.)

questions.question: Which word is an ADVERB in 'He works hard every day.'?
questions.explanation: 'Hard' describes the verb 'works' (HOW he works), so here it is an adverb even though it does not end in -ly.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the modifier correctly?

choices.D: The roses are a sweetly bunch.

questions.explanation: After the linking verb 'smell,' the adjective 'sweet' describes the noun 'roses,' not the action.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The team performed ___ in the final round.'
questions.explanation: The adverb 'perfectly' describes the verb 'performed' (HOW they performed).

questions.question: Which word is an ADJECTIVE in 'A nervous student raised a shaky hand.'?
questions.explanation: 'Nervous' describes the noun 'student,' so it is an adjective. ('Shaky' also describes a noun, but 'nervous' is the listed adjective choice.)

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The chef chopped the onions ___.'
questions.explanation: The adverb 'neatly' describes the verb 'chopped' (HOW he chopped).

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'They built a ___ tower out of blocks.'
questions.explanation: The adjective 'tall' describes the noun 'tower.'

questions.question: Which word is an ADVERB in 'The rain fell heavily all night.'?
questions.explanation: 'Heavily' describes the verb 'fell' (HOW the rain fell), so it is an adverb.

questions.question: Which sentence uses both an adjective and an adverb correctly?
questions.explanation: The adjective 'quiet' describes the noun 'student,' and the adverb 'quietly' describes the verb 'read.'

questions.question: In 'The really old map crumbled easily,' which word is an ADVERB describing a verb?
questions.explanation: 'Easily' describes the verb 'crumbled' (HOW it crumbled). ('Really' is an adverb too, but it describes the adjective 'old,' not a verb.)

5-2.title: Comparative & Superlative Forms
5-2.learn:
HOW TO USE COMPARATIVE AND SUPERLATIVE FORMS

Use the COMPARATIVE to compare TWO things — add -er or use 'more': 'faster,' 'more careful.'
Use the SUPERLATIVE to compare THREE or more — add -est or use 'most': 'fastest,' 'most careful.'

Example 1 — Two things (comparative): 'She is the taller of the two sisters.'
Comparing two, so use 'taller' (-er).

Example 2 — Three or more (superlative): 'She is the tallest in the class.'
Comparing many, so use 'tallest' (-est).

Example 3 — Longer words use 'more'/'most': 'careful' becomes 'more careful' (two things) and 'most careful' (three or more), NOT 'carefuller.'

Never double up: don't say 'more taller' or 'most fastest.' Use ONLY -er/-est OR more/most, not both.
Irregular forms: good → better → best; bad → worse → worst.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'A cheetah is ___ than a lion.'
questions.explanation: Comparing two animals uses the comparative 'faster.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'Mount Everest is the ___ mountain on Earth.'
questions.explanation: Comparing many mountains uses the superlative 'tallest.'

questions.question: Which is the comparative form of 'big'?
questions.explanation: The comparative form of 'big' adds -er to become 'bigger.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'This is the ___ book I have ever read.'
questions.explanation: Comparing all the books she has read uses the superlative 'most interesting.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'Of the two routes, this one is ___.'
questions.explanation: Comparing two routes uses the comparative 'shorter.'

questions.question: Which sentence is CORRECT?

choices.A: She is more taller than her brother.
choices.B: She is taller than her brother.
choices.C: She is tallest than her brother.
choices.D: She is most tall than her brother.

questions.explanation: Comparing two people uses 'taller' alone; 'more taller' is a double comparative error.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'My grade this term is ___ than last term.'
questions.explanation: The comparative of the irregular word 'good' is 'better.'

questions.question: Which sentence has a comparison ERROR?

choices.A: This is the worst movie of the year.
choices.C: He is the most fastest runner.
choices.D: She is more careful than I am.

questions.explanation: 'Most fastest' doubles the superlative; it should be just 'fastest.'

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'Of all three teams, ours played the ___.'
questions.explanation: Comparing three teams uses the superlative of 'well,' which is the irregular 'best.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a superlative for three or more items?

choices.A: This is the more delicious meal of them all.
choices.B: This is the most delicious meal of them all.
choices.C: This is the deliciousest meal of them all.
choices.D: This is the most deliciousest meal of them all.

questions.explanation: The longer word 'delicious' forms its superlative with 'most': 'most delicious.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'My backpack is ___ than yours.'
questions.explanation: Comparing two backpacks uses the comparative 'heavier.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'That was the ___ day of the whole year.'
questions.explanation: Comparing all the days of the year uses the superlative 'coldest.'

questions.question: Which is the comparative form of 'small'?
questions.explanation: The comparative of 'small' adds -er to become 'smaller.'

questions.question: Which is the superlative form of 'loud'?
questions.explanation: The superlative of 'loud' adds -est to become 'loudest.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'A whale is ___ than a dolphin.'
questions.explanation: Comparing two animals uses the comparative 'larger.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'She is the ___ player on the entire team.'
questions.explanation: Comparing all players on the team uses the superlative of 'good,' which is the irregular 'best.'

questions.question: Which is the comparative form of 'happy'?
questions.explanation: A short word ending in -y changes to -ier: 'happy' becomes 'happier.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'Of my two pencils, this one is ___.'
questions.explanation: Comparing two pencils uses the comparative 'sharper.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'Today's homework was ___ than yesterday's.'
questions.explanation: The longer word 'difficult' forms its comparative with 'more': 'more difficult' (comparing two days).

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'This puzzle is the ___ one in the book.'
questions.explanation: Comparing all puzzles in the book uses the superlative 'most challenging' for the longer word.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'My cold is ___ today than it was yesterday.'
questions.explanation: The comparative of the irregular word 'bad' is 'worse.'

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'That was the ___ storm we have ever had.'
questions.explanation: The superlative of the irregular word 'bad' is 'worst' (comparing all storms).

questions.question: Which sentence is CORRECT?

choices.A: This rope is more longer than that one.
choices.B: This rope is longer than that one.
choices.C: This rope is longest than that one.
choices.D: This rope is most long than that one.

questions.explanation: Comparing two ropes uses 'longer' alone; 'more longer' is a double comparative error.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'Of the three desserts, the cake was the ___.'
questions.explanation: Comparing three desserts uses the superlative 'sweetest.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'A bicycle is ___ than a car.'
questions.explanation: Comparing two things uses the comparative 'slower.'

questions.question: Which is the superlative form of 'beautiful'?
questions.explanation: The longer word 'beautiful' forms its superlative with 'most': 'most beautiful.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'He jumped ___ than anyone else in the contest.'
questions.explanation: The word 'than' signals a comparison between him and each other person, so the comparative 'higher' is correct.

questions.question: Which sentence has a comparison ERROR?

choices.A: She is the smartest girl in the class.
choices.B: This box is heavier than that one.
choices.C: He is the most strongest boy on the team.
choices.D: My dog is friendlier than yours.

questions.explanation: 'Most strongest' doubles the superlative; it should be just 'strongest.'

questions.question: Which sentence has a comparison ERROR?

choices.A: This test was easier than the last one.
choices.B: This test was more easier than the last one.
choices.C: This was the easiest test all year.
choices.D: She finished faster than I did.

questions.explanation: 'More easier' doubles the comparative; it should be just 'easier.'

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'Of all my classes, math is the ___.'
questions.explanation: Comparing all classes uses the superlative of 'good,' which is the irregular 'best.'

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'My handwriting is ___ than my brother's, but Dad's is the worst of all.'
questions.explanation: Comparing two people (me and my brother) uses the comparative 'worse.'

questions.question: Which sentence correctly uses a comparative for two things?

choices.A: This trail is the more steep of the two.
choices.B: This trail is the steeper of the two.
choices.C: This trail is the steepest of the two.
choices.D: This trail is the most steep of the two.

questions.explanation: Comparing two trails uses 'steeper' (-er), not the superlative or a doubled form.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'A turtle is ___ than a rabbit.'
questions.explanation: Comparing two animals uses the comparative 'slower.'

questions.question: Which is the superlative form of 'tall'?
questions.explanation: The superlative of 'tall' adds -est to become 'tallest.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'This river is the ___ in the country.'
questions.explanation: Comparing all rivers in the country uses the superlative 'longest.'

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'My new shoes are ___ than my old ones.'
questions.explanation: The longer word 'comfortable' forms its comparative with 'more': 'more comfortable' (comparing two pairs).

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'Of all the puppies, the spotted one is the ___.'
questions.explanation: Comparing all the puppies uses the superlative 'cutest.'

questions.question: Which is the comparative form of 'expensive'?
questions.explanation: The longer word 'expensive' forms its comparative with 'more': 'more expensive.'

questions.question: Which sentence is CORRECT?

choices.A: She is the most funniest person I know.
choices.B: She is the funniest person I know.
choices.C: She is the more funniest person I know.
choices.D: She is the most funny person I know.

questions.explanation: The short word 'funny' forms its superlative as 'funniest'; adding 'most' would double it.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'This summer is ___ than last summer, but two years ago was the hottest.'
questions.explanation: Comparing two summers uses the comparative 'hotter.'

5-3.title: Misplaced & Dangling Modifiers
5-3.learn:
HOW TO FIX MISPLACED AND DANGLING MODIFIERS

A MODIFIER is a word or phrase that describes something. Put it RIGHT NEXT to the word it describes, or the sentence gets confusing or silly.

Example 1 — Misplaced: 'I saw a dog walking to school.'
This sounds like the DOG walked to school! Fix by moving the modifier: 'Walking to school, I saw a dog.' Now it clearly describes 'I.'

Example 2 — Misplaced word: 'She almost drove her kids to school every day.'
'Almost' is misplaced — did she almost drive them? Fix: 'She drove her kids to school almost every day.'

Example 3 — Dangling: 'Running to the bus, my backpack fell.'
This says the BACKPACK was running! The describing phrase has nothing real to attach to. Fix: 'Running to the bus, I dropped my backpack.'

To fix: ask 'WHO or WHAT is doing this?' Then put that word right after the describing phrase, or rewrite so the modifier clearly matches the right word.

questions.question: Why is 'I saw a deer driving down the road' confusing?

choices.A: It sounds like the deer was driving.
choices.C: It is missing a comma only.

questions.explanation: The modifier 'driving down the road' is placed next to 'deer,' making it sound like the deer drove.

questions.question: Which is the BEST fix for 'Walking to school, the rain soaked me.'?

choices.A: Walking to school, the rain soaked me.
choices.B: Walking to school, I got soaked by the rain.
choices.C: The rain walking to school soaked me.
choices.D: Soaked by walking, the rain to school.

questions.explanation: Adding 'I' right after the phrase fixes the dangling modifier, since the rain cannot walk.

questions.question: Where should a modifier be placed?

choices.A: At the very end of every sentence
choices.B: Right next to the word it describes
choices.C: As far as possible from the word it describes

questions.explanation: A modifier should sit right next to the word it describes to avoid confusion.

questions.question: Which sentence has a MISPLACED modifier?

choices.A: She wore a hat on her head that was red.
choices.B: She wore a red hat on her head.
choices.C: On her head she wore a red hat.

questions.explanation: 'That was red' is placed next to 'head,' making it sound like her head was red; it should describe the hat.

questions.question: Which is the BEST fix for 'Covered in mud, Mom told me to take a bath.'?

choices.A: Covered in mud, Mom told me to take a bath.
choices.B: Mom told me, covered in mud, to take a bath.
choices.C: Because I was covered in mud, Mom told me to take a bath.
choices.D: Covered in mud told me Mom to bath.

questions.explanation: Rewriting makes clear that 'I' was covered in mud, not Mom, fixing the dangling modifier.

questions.question: Which sentence is clear and correct?

choices.A: Running fast, the finish line came into view for the runner.
choices.B: Running fast, the runner saw the finish line come into view.
choices.C: The finish line running fast came into view.
choices.D: Came into view running fast the finish line.

questions.explanation: The runner is the one running fast, so placing 'the runner' right after the phrase makes it clear.

questions.question: What is wrong with 'He served sandwiches to the children on paper plates'?

choices.A: It sounds like the children are on paper plates.

questions.explanation: 'On paper plates' is placed next to 'children,' making it sound like the children are on the plates; it should describe the sandwiches.

questions.question: Which is the BEST revision of 'After finishing the homework, the TV was turned on.'?

choices.A: After finishing the homework, the TV was turned on.
choices.B: After finishing the homework, I turned on the TV.
choices.C: The TV after finishing homework was turned on.
choices.D: Turned on the TV after finishing the homework was.

questions.explanation: A TV cannot finish homework, so adding 'I' as the doer fixes the dangling modifier.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly places the word 'only'?

choices.C: Only I ate one cookie said no one.

questions.explanation: Placing 'only' right before 'one cookie' makes clear exactly how many were eaten.

questions.question: Which sentence has NO modifier problem?

choices.A: Barking loudly, the mail carrier was scared by the dog.
choices.B: Barking loudly, the dog scared the mail carrier.
choices.C: The mail carrier barking loudly scared the dog.
choices.D: Scared by the dog, the barking was loud.

questions.explanation: The dog is the one barking, so 'Barking loudly' correctly attaches to 'the dog.'

questions.question: Why is 'I found a wallet walking through the park' confusing?

choices.A: It sounds like the wallet was walking.

questions.explanation: The phrase 'walking through the park' sits next to 'wallet,' making it sound like the wallet was walking.

questions.question: Which is the BEST fix for 'Running late, the bus was missed by Sam.'?

choices.A: Running late, the bus was missed by Sam.
choices.B: The bus running late was missed by Sam.
choices.C: Running late, Sam missed the bus.
choices.D: Missed the bus Sam running late.

questions.explanation: A bus cannot be 'running late' here in the intended sense, so adding 'Sam' as the one running late fixes the dangling modifier.

questions.question: Why should a modifier sit next to the word it describes?

choices.B: So the sentence stays clear and not confusing
choices.C: Because modifiers always go at the end
choices.D: It is just a style choice with no real reason

questions.explanation: Keeping a modifier next to the word it describes keeps the meaning clear and prevents silly or confusing sentences.

questions.question: Why is 'She gave a snack to the dog in a plastic bowl' confusing?

choices.A: It sounds like the dog is in a plastic bowl.

questions.explanation: 'In a plastic bowl' is placed next to 'dog,' making it sound like the dog is in the bowl; it should describe the snack.

questions.question: Which is the BEST fix for 'Frozen solid, I could not open the door.'?

choices.A: Frozen solid, I could not open the door.
choices.B: I frozen solid could not open the door.
choices.C: Could not open the door I frozen solid.
choices.D: Because the lock was frozen solid, I could not open the door.

questions.explanation: The person was not frozen solid; rewriting shows the lock was frozen, fixing the dangling modifier.

questions.question: Which sentence has a MISPLACED modifier?

choices.A: He read a book about sharks with a torn cover.
choices.B: He read a book with a torn cover about sharks.
choices.C: He read a torn book about sharks.
choices.D: He read a book about sharks.

questions.explanation: 'With a torn cover' is placed next to 'sharks,' making it sound like the sharks had a torn cover; it should describe the book.

questions.question: Which is the BEST fix for 'Tired from the trip, the bed looked inviting to Maria.'?

choices.A: Tired from the trip, the bed looked inviting to Maria.
choices.B: The bed tired from the trip looked inviting to Maria.
choices.C: Tired from the trip, Maria thought the bed looked inviting.
choices.D: Looked inviting the bed Maria tired from the trip.

questions.explanation: A bed cannot be tired from a trip; making 'Maria' the one who is tired fixes the dangling modifier.

questions.question: Which sentence is clear and correct?

choices.A: Hidden under the bed, Jake found his missing shoe.
choices.B: Hidden under the bed, Jake searched the room.
choices.C: Jake found his missing shoe hidden under the bed.
choices.D: Under the bed Jake hidden found his shoe.

questions.explanation: The shoe was hidden under the bed, so placing 'hidden under the bed' next to 'shoe' keeps the meaning clear.

questions.question: What is wrong with 'The teacher returned the tests to the students with red marks'?

choices.A: It sounds like the students have red marks.

questions.explanation: 'With red marks' is placed next to 'students,' making it sound like the students have red marks; it should describe the tests.

questions.question: Which is the BEST revision of 'While watching TV, the cookies burned in the oven.'?

choices.A: While watching TV, the cookies burned in the oven.
choices.B: The cookies while watching TV burned in the oven.
choices.C: Burned in the oven the cookies while watching TV.
choices.D: While I was watching TV, the cookies burned in the oven.

questions.explanation: Cookies cannot watch TV; naming 'I' as the watcher fixes the dangling modifier.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly places the word 'just'?

choices.A: I just want one slice of pizza.
choices.B: I want just one slice of pizza.
choices.C: Just I want one slice of pizza.
choices.D: I want one just slice of pizza.

questions.explanation: Placing 'just' right before 'one slice' makes clear that the amount wanted is only one slice.

questions.question: Which is the BEST fix for 'Smiling proudly, the trophy was handed to the winner.'?

choices.A: Smiling proudly, the trophy was handed to the winner.
choices.B: The trophy smiling proudly was handed to the winner.
choices.C: Smiling proudly, the coach handed the trophy to the winner.
choices.D: Handed to the winner smiling proudly the trophy.

questions.explanation: A trophy cannot smile proudly; naming 'the coach' as the one smiling fixes the dangling modifier.

questions.question: Which sentence has a MISPLACED modifier?

choices.A: We watched the parade standing on the corner.
choices.B: Standing on the corner, we watched the parade.
choices.C: We stood on the corner and watched the parade.
choices.D: From the corner, we watched the parade.

questions.explanation: 'Standing on the corner' is placed next to 'parade,' making it sound like the parade was standing on the corner; it should describe 'we.'

questions.question: Why is 'He almost ran the whole marathon' different from 'He ran almost the whole marathon'?

choices.A: 'Almost ran' suggests he nearly did not run at all, while 'almost the whole' means he ran most of it.
choices.B: They mean exactly the same thing.
choices.D: Only the second one is grammatical.

questions.explanation: Where 'almost' sits changes the meaning: next to 'ran' it limits the verb; next to 'the whole' it limits the distance.

questions.question: Which sentence is clear and correct?

choices.A: Buzzing around the kitchen, I swatted the fly.
choices.B: Buzzing around the kitchen, the fly was swatted by me.
choices.C: I swatted the fly buzzing around the kitchen.
choices.D: The fly I buzzing around the kitchen swatted.

questions.explanation: The fly was buzzing, so placing 'buzzing around the kitchen' next to 'fly' keeps the meaning clear.

questions.question: Which is the BEST fix for 'Excited about the game, the snacks were ready early.'?

choices.A: Excited about the game, the snacks were ready early.
choices.B: The snacks excited about the game were ready early.
choices.C: Ready early the snacks excited about the game.
choices.D: Excited about the game, we had the snacks ready early.

questions.explanation: Snacks cannot be excited; naming 'we' as the excited ones fixes the dangling modifier.

questions.question: Which sentence correctly places the word 'nearly'?

choices.A: I nearly waited two hours for the bus.
choices.B: I waited nearly two hours for the bus.
choices.C: Nearly I waited two hours for the bus.
choices.D: I waited two nearly hours for the bus.

questions.explanation: Placing 'nearly' right before 'two hours' makes clear the length of time waited.

questions.question: Which sentence has a MISPLACED modifier?

choices.A: She handed a balloon to the boy that was bright red.
choices.B: She handed a bright red balloon to the boy.
